cards.text: Baker, these are the words of a man named Amos, and what he saw concerns Israel. It came two years before the earthquake, when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel. So who is this guy?

cards.question: Amos is about to carry the LORD's words. What does Amos do for work?

cards.text: A sheepherder from Tekoa, and I'm a cookie stamper who did years in a junk drawer, so who am I to judge a résumé? Then Amos opens his mouth: "The LORD roars from Zion." Not a whisper, friend. ROARS.

cards.question: When the LORD roars from Zion, what happens to the land?

answers.text: The pastures mourn and Carmel withers

cards.text: Then the LORD speaks, and He starts with Damascus, the head of Aram (Isaiah 7:8). He says, "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment."

cards.question: The LORD says He will not revoke His judgment on Damascus. What does that mean?

cards.text: And the LORD says why: Damascus threshed Gilead with sledges of iron. A threshing sledge is a tool made for grain, and they took it to Gilead.

cards.question: The LORD names the house of Hazael and the citadels of Ben-hadad, kings of Aram (2 Kings 13:3). What will He send upon them?

cards.text: Then He gets specific: the gates of Damascus come down, and the rulers in the Valley of Aven and Beth-eden get cut off. I once gave a baker directions by pointing my mustache and saying "over there," and friend, the LORD does not do "over there."

cards.question: True or false: after the gates of Damascus come down, the LORD says the people of Aram get to stay in their land.

cards.text: Next up is Gaza, and there it is, that line again: three transgressions, even four, and no taking back the judgment. Hear it twice and you know it like the beep of your own oven timer.

cards.question: What does the LORD say Gaza did?

answers.text: They exiled a whole population to Edom
They tore down the altar at Bethel
They poisoned the wells of Judah

cards.text: So fire comes upon the walls of Gaza. Then the LORD names Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, like a whole group chat getting called out one name at a time.

cards.question: After Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, what does the LORD say about whoever is left of the Philistines?
Next is Tyre, and Tyre also delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom. What else does the LORD say Tyre broke?

cards.text: And Tyre gets the same sentence: fire upon its walls to consume its citadels. Three nations in, and nobody's walked away clean.

Next on the list is Edom, the people who came from Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Genesis 25:24-26; 36:1). And that line again: three transgressions, even four. By now, baker, you could say it right along with Him.

cards.question: Edom's charge sounds personal. What does the LORD say Edom did?

answers.text: Pursued his brother with the sword

cards.question: True or false: the LORD says Edom's anger flared up once and then cooled off.

cards.text: So fire falls on Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah. Teman, Bozrah, friend, I need a map just to keep up, and I live on a planet barely big enough for my bakery.
Then come the Ammonites. What they did is hard to even say out loud: they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead.

cards.question: The Ammonites did that to the women of Gilead. What does the LORD say they did it for?

cards.text: So the LORD will kindle a fire in the walls of Rabbah, the Ammonite city (2 Samuel 12:26). It comes with war cries on the day of battle and a violent wind on the day of tempest.

cards.question: What does the LORD say happens to the Ammonite king?

answers.text: He goes into exile with his princes

cards.text: Then comes Moab, with that same line again. This time the charge is about what Moab did to the king of Edom.

cards.question: What does the LORD say Moab did to the king of Edom?

answers.text: Took his crown as a prize

cards.question: Moab's sin was against Edom's king, not against Israel or Judah. True or false: the LORD still judges Moab for it.

cards.text: So fire comes against Moab, on the citadels of Kerioth. Moab will die in tumult, with war cries and the sound of the ram's horn.

cards.question: The LORD will cut off the ruler of Moab. Who goes down with him?

cards.text: And now the list comes home: the next name is Judah, where Amos's own town of Tekoa sits (2 Chronicles 11:5-6). It's like nodding along in a meeting while everybody else gets called out, and then the boss says YOUR name.

cards.question: What is the LORD's charge against Judah?

answers.text: They reject the Law of the LORD
They attacked Edom with the sword

cards.text: Did you catch that, friend? Every nation before was judged for what it did to people, but Judah's charge is about what it did with the Law of the LORD.

cards.question: Judah is led astray by the lies their fathers walked in. What does that say about Judah's problem?

cards.text: So Judah gets the same sentence as the nations: fire upon Judah to consume the citadels of Jerusalem. And friend, Amos isn't done talking yet.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 3 quotes "The LORD roars from Zion.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: Stop 1, card 5 quotes "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment.", which isn't the exact BSB wording.

rule.text: Quotes: Quotation marks around Bible words mean the exact BSB wording, punctuation included.

findings.problem: The card uses Tekoa, which comes from Amos 1:1, but it cites only Amos 1:2. The citation should be Amos 1:1-2.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: the résumé joke, the quote, "Not a whisper, friend." and "ROARS." It is not the opening card.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Only the right answer has a proper place name (Carmel), so it sounds more like the Bible than "The rivers flood the valleys" and "The fields burst into bloom."

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card spends a sentence defining a threshing sledge ("A threshing sledge is a tool made for grain"). It should leave that to the dictionary pop-up and use the words for the moment itself.

rule.text: Don't spend card words explaining a hard word. Hard words get a dictionary pop-up (definitions.md, made after the cards).

findings.problem: Several cards tell the LORD's announced judgments as if they are happening. The text says what the LORD will do ("I will send fire," "I will break down," "I will cut off"). Stop 1 card 9 says the gates "come down" and the rulers "get cut off." Stop 1 card 10 says "after the gates of Damascus come down." Stop 1 card 13 says "fire comes upon the walls of Gaza." Stop 2 card 4 says "fire falls on Teman." Stop 2 card 12 says "fire comes against Moab." Stop 2 card 7 gets it right with "the LORD will kindle."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Gaza (stop 1 card 11), Tyre (stop 1 card 15), the Ammonites (stop 2 card 5) and Moab (stop 2 card 9) are never introduced when they first appear. Damascus and Edom are introduced.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: The answers are not the same kind of thing. The right answer is an agreement (a covenant). The wrong answers are physical objects (walls, an altar). The right answer is the only one that naturally goes with being broken in a relational sense.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: Most of the choice cards in stop 1 can't be reasoned out from earlier cards: Amos's job (card 2), what happens to the land (card 4), what the LORD sends (card 8), Gaza's charge (card 12) and what else Tyre broke (card 15). That is 5 of 8.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates stop 1: 7 multiple choice, 1 true or false and no fill in the blank.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates stop 2: 7 multiple choice, 2 true or false and no fill in the blank.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says Edom is "the people who came from Esau" and cites Genesis 36:1. That verse identifies Esau as Edom but doesn't say the Edomites descended from him. Genesis 36:9 ("Esau, the father of the Edomites") supports the claim.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The question says "The Ammonites did that to the women of Gilead," and "that" points back to story card 5, which is no longer on screen.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: Story card 9 already gives away the answer. It tells the baker Moab gets "that same line again," which includes "I will not revoke My judgment," and it calls what Moab did "the charge." Whether the LORD still judges Moab is settled before the question is asked.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The card ends with "Amos isn't done talking yet." The passage's story group is none, and prep-walkthrough.md calls for this line only when the passage is in a story group and isn't the last passage in it. But the LORD's message clearly continues into Amos 2:6, with the same formula aimed at Israel. papa-dorin.md says: "When a passage's story or teaching continues in the next passage, he says so at the end."
findings.question: When a passage has no story group but its teaching plainly continues in the next passage, as Amos 1:1-2:5 does into 2:6, should the walkthrough end with the line that the teaching isn't done? Or should this passage be in a story group with the passage that follows?
